title: How To Use Your Teacherly Sense
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Drawing on Malcolm Gladwell's concept from Blink of experts recognizing truths instantly without being able to explain why, Linsin names an equivalent teacher instinct -- the 'teacherly sense' -- the flash of certainty that a lesson didn't land, that a student entering the room is about to misbehave, or that someone nearby is being bullied. He argues this sense is built through active observation over time and becomes usable through a deliberate two-step process: first, become an astute, constantly observing teacher (following the management plan consistently, learning students' strengths and weaknesses, matching lessons precisely to their needs), and second, pause the moment the sense fires rather than reacting on impulse or ignoring it, using that pause to gather more information before acting. He illustrates the pause-then-act sequence with a concrete example -- sensing rising excitability as students enter and pausing to decide whether to redirect with calming breaths before the energy turns into misbehavior. The underlying claim is that this instinct is a genuine, trainable advantage available to every teacher, not a mystical talent limited to a few.
points: Names the instinctive flash of certainty teachers get about a lesson failing, a student about to misbehave, or hidden bullying as the 'teacherly sense,' drawing on Gladwell's Blink.
Build the sense through active, constant observation -- consistently following the management plan and learning individual students' strengths and weaknesses.
When the sense fires, pause before acting rather than reacting impulsively or ignoring it; the pause lets you gather more information and decide deliberately.
Frames the teacherly sense as a trainable skill available to any teacher through experience, not an innate or mystical talent.
quotes: In Malcom Gladwell’s 2003 book Blink , he describes how experts can know what they know but not know why they know it.
They experience a flash of recognition or vision of truth—a blink moment—based on years of past experience and know it to be accurate. As teachers we have these blink moments often.
By trusting your teacherly sense, you can act. You can stop what is coming before it arrives. You can alter your lesson, remind the student, or protect the bullied.
The second step is to pause when it hits you. Blink moments happen immediately. If you ignore them or react without thinking, then they’re of no use.

You must pause first. Ascertain what it’s telling you. Then act. The pause can also allow you to take in more information, like when you notice something strange about the way students are milling around.
